cur:objects2-paschal-enamel-cross.summary: This small cross-shaped reliquary for a fragment of the True Cross is covered with cloisonné enamel scenes of the childhood of Christ on a translucent green ground: the Annunciation and Visitation in the upper arm, the Nativity with the bathing of the Child at the centre, the journey to Bethlehem and the Adoration of the Magi in the side arms, and the Presentation in the Temple and the Baptism below. It is among the earliest surviving narrative enamels of the Christian world.
facts: The museum label calls it the 'Enamelled Cross of Paschal I'; it was preserved in its own reliquary case among the relics of the Lateran's Sancta Sanctorum chapel.
Whether it was made in Rome or in Byzantium is disputed; the museum label dates it to about the first quarter of the 9th century.
cur:objects2-paschal-enamel-cross.notes: Scene identifications are from the visible enamels and the label's general description ('episodes of the infancy of Christ').

Q541376.summary: In a crush of bodies lit by a single lantern, Judas presses his kiss upon Christ while armoured soldiers close in. Christ does not resist: his hands are folded and his eyes are lowered in sorrow rather than fear. Caravaggio compresses the betrayal in Gethsemane into a frozen instant of violence, intimacy and surrender.
facts: The painting was lost for nearly two centuries; it was rediscovered in 1990 hanging in the Jesuit house in Dublin, where it had long been taken for a copy by Gerard van Honthorst.
The man at the far right holding up the lantern is widely thought to be a self-portrait of Caravaggio.
It was painted for the Roman nobleman Ciriaco Mattei, whose family account books record a payment of 125 scudi for it on 2 January 1603.
